results.content: # Statistical Power, MDE, and Designing Statistical Tests. One topic has surfaced in my ten years of developing statistical tools, consulting, and participating in discussions and conversations with CRO & A/B testing practitioners as causing the most confusion and that is statistical power and the related concept of minimum detectable effect (MDE). A major reason for the misuse and misunderstanding of statistical power can be found in the textbook approach to designing statistical tests. The power of a statistical test is a function of its sample size and confidence threshold over the range of all possible values of the parameters of interest. The statistical power of a test is a function of its sample size and confidence threshold showing the probability to reject the null hypothesis over all possible values of the parameter of interest. ## The power level of a test. When one speaks of “statistical power of a test” it typically refers to “the power *level* at a given effect size of interest” instead of the power function over the entire set of possible parameter values.

results.title: Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) Calculator | MetricGate
results.content: The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest true difference between a treatment and a control group that an experiment can reliably detect given its sample size, significance level, and statistical power. It is the complement of sample size calculation: rather than asking how many observations you need to detect a given effect, MDE asks what effect size you can detect with the observations you have. If your MDE is 5 percentage points but you only expect a 1 percentage-point lift, launching the experiment would waste resources — you would be highly unlikely to see statistical significance even if the effect is real. For a two-proportion z-test, the MDE is derived from the sample size formula by solving for the effect size: *MDE ≈ (z\_(1−α/2) + z\_(1−β)) · √(2 · p̄ · (1 − p̄) / n)*, where *p̄* is the baseline conversion rate, *n* is the sample size per group, and the z-scores correspond to the chosen significance level and power.

results.title: Statistical Power, MDE, and Designing Statistical Tests | by Georgi Georgiev | Medium
results.content: > **The power level of a statistical test is defined as the probability of observing a *p*-value statistically significant at a certain threshold α if a true effect of a certain magnitude μ 1 is in fact present.**. The generic formula for the power level of a statistical test at a given true effect size is:. If, instead, the minimum effect of interest is 5%, the power level of the same statistical test is just ~41%. First, the initial confidence threshold is defined, then an initial value for the minimum effect of interest is chosen without regard for power, and finally power levels for the MEI at various test durations / sample sizes are examined. In other words, with an *already specified* test (in terms of sample size, confidence threshold, and variance) a minimum detectable effect can be obtained at any *power level of interest* such that:. > **The minimum detectable effect is the true effect size at which a given test achieves a power level of interest.**. * a test will not produce a statistically significant outcome if the true effect size is less than the MDE at some chosen power level. * if the observed effect size is less than the MDE at some chosen power level, it will not be statistically significant (or if it is, something is wrong with the validity of the test). The reason we prefer minimum effect of interest in the scenario of planning an A/B test, and minimum detectable effect when examining a test with already specified characteristics and a chosen power level is that however complicated the specification of a minimum effect of interest may be, specifying a power level of interest instead **does not fit the typical process of designing A/B tests** and likely most experiments in other fields. It complements that with an understanding of the power level of a test as only specified at a given minimum effect of interest, making the two-way interaction between these concepts explicit which exposes deficiencies in the textbook approach to designing statistical tests. The complicated interplay between the variables involved in planning an A/B test using risk/reward optimization and the feedback loops in determining a test’s confidence threshold, minimum effect of interest, and sample size are made explicit.

# Power Analysis for A/B Tests: Metrics, MDE & Sample Size. Power analysis is the planning step that answers that — before time, traffic, or participants are spent.*. ## Power, alpha, effect size, sample size: the four dials. A power analysis links four quantities. * **Statistical power (1 — β):** the chance your test detects a real effect. Many teams target **80%** power; 90% is common when missing a true effect would be costly. Lower α reduces false positives but also reduces power unless you add more data. Defining effect size keeps you from chasing trivial wins. * **Sample size (N):** the number of observations per group required to achieve your chosen power at your chosen α for your effect size. These dials move together: bigger effects, looser α, and larger samples increase power; sloppier measurement and noisier metrics decrease it.
